newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil minister sees changes, vague on details.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil minister sees changes, vague on details.

text.p: Russian Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov, a natural gas executive little known to foreign oil investors, said on Thursday that he would create "rules of the game" and new policies for Russia's energy sectors.
In an interview with Reuters, which aides said was his first with the press, Rodionov said: "Of course there will be new polices. Life moves on."
Rodionov, 45, was appointed by President Boris Yeltsin last month after predecessor Yuri Shafranik left to chair the board of the Tyumen Oil Company.

The new minister has mingled with Western oil men at industry receptions and meetings -- but he is a mystery to foreign executives, who say they need his blessing to drill for some of the world's last untapped reserves.

Rodionov, who headed a St Petersburg subsidiary of the Gazprom natural gas monopoly, has inherited a different world than did Shafranik, who became minister in early 1993 after running the oil-rich Tyumen region.

Russia's oil sector was transformed during Shafranik's tenure, when Yeltsin turned state-run production associations into privatised, vertically-integrated companies but left Gazprom, the world's largest gas producer, a monopoly.
"We will accordingly correct those realities which we have today," Rodionov said. "We should have started with the rules, but rather we just started playing the game without any.
"But I haven't come here to dismantle things. We must set up regulators to develop the economy, not to oppress it."
He said Russia, which depends on its oil exports for much of its hard currency earnings, would not and could not significantly increase oil export levels soon.

"We should not try to compete with OPEC (the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries) in the oil trade, but to build a competitive economy that can compete with the United States or anybody else," he said.
Rodionov said new changes were on the horizon in Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer, with output last year of about 306 million tonnes.
"The rules of the game are normal laws and normal price, tariff and tax policies," he said, declining to be specific.
Asked if he was a capitalist at heart, he said: "In principle, yes. I don't see any other way."
He added: "Privatisation has taken place as it did -- we now have the reality we have created. I will neither hasten nor slow the process."

Asked about the tens of billions of dollars Western oil companies have said they plan to invest in oil-output sharing deals if the terms are right, Rodionov said: "It in no way hinders things and some ways helps."
But he said he would look at each project individually.

"I don't intend to break any contracts," he said. "We will look at each project individually, its merits, its expediency. We will decide whether some of our reserves should be developed now or in 20 or 50 years."

He said foreign oil investment projects should consider the exploration and infrastructure work done by the Soviet Union. Valuing such work is often a stumbling block to Western oil deals planned here.

Rodionov was somewhat critical of Russia's shares for loans tenders, in which stakes in oil and other firms were sold for low prices to bidders that seemed to be pre-determined winners. "The concept behind them was all right, but they shouldn't have been done so fast. These firms are worth far more," he said.

He said more changes could be in the works for Russia's new oil companies, but Gazprom would remain intact. "Maybe some mergers will take place with (oil) companies -- each has to decide for itself whether to merge or to devolve."
He said Gazprom should open up its pipelines to domestic competitors and he welcomed investment by foreign electricity generators.
